back: The positive charge of the atom is uniformly distributed throughout its volume, with the negatively charged electrons embedded in it like seeds in a watermelon - the plum pudding model (1898).
The entire positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in a small volume called the nucleus, with electrons revolving around it as planets revolve around the sun.
The perpendicular distance of the initial velocity vector of the alpha-particle from the centre of the nucleus. Small b gives large scattering; large b gives almost no deflection.
Head-on collision: b is minimum and the alpha-particle rebounds back, theta = pi. Very large b: it passes nearly undeviated, theta = 0.
d = 2Ze^2/(4 pi epsilon_0 K), obtained by setting the initial kinetic energy equal to the Coulomb potential energy (1/4 pi epsilon_0)(2e)(Ze)/d.

front: Size of nucleus versus size of atom
back: Nucleus about 10^-15 m to 10^-14 m; atom about 10^-10 m. The nucleus is 10,000 to 100,000 times smaller, so most of the atom is empty space.
Most alpha-particles pass straight through; about 0.14% scatter by more than 1 degree; about 1 in 8000 deflect by more than 90 degrees.

front: Why the classical Rutherford atom must collapse
back: An electron in a circular orbit is accelerating, so it must radiate; its energy falls continuously and it spirals into the nucleus. The atom cannot be stable.

front: Why the classical atom gives a continuous spectrum
back: The emitted frequency equals the frequency of revolution, which changes continuously as the electron spirals inward - so the emission is continuous, not a set of lines.
An electron can revolve in certain stable orbits without emitting radiant energy. Each atom has definite stable states of definite total energy, called stationary states.
L = nh/2 pi, n = 1, 2, 3, ... : the angular momentum of the orbiting electron is quantised in units of h/2 pi.
On a transition from a higher to a lower state a photon is emitted: h nu = E_i - E_f.

front: Radius of the nth Bohr orbit
back: r_n = n^2 h^2 epsilon_0/(pi m e^2) = n^2 a_0, with a_0 = 5.3 x 10^-11 m. Radius grows as n^2.

front: Speed of the electron in the nth orbit
back: v_n = e^2/(2 epsilon_0 n h) = 2.2 x 10^6 / n m/s. Speed falls as 1/n.

front: Energy of the nth Bohr orbit

back: 13.6 eV - the energy needed to take the electron from the ground state (n = 1) to rest at infinity (E = 0 eV).

front: Excitation energies from the ground state

back: Emission: bright lines on a dark background, from an excited rarefied gas. Absorption: dark lines at the same wavelengths on a continuous bright spectrum, after white light passes through the gas.
Lyman ends on n_f = 1 (UV); Balmer on n_f = 2 (visible); Paschen n_f = 3, Brackett n_f = 4, Pfund n_f = 5 (all infrared).
1/lambda = R(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2), with R = m e^4/(8 epsilon_0^2 h^3 c) = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1. It follows from E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV together with h nu = E_i - E_f.

The electron is a particle wave on its orbit; a standing wave exists only if the circumference is an integral number of wavelengths, 2 pi r_n = n lambda. With lambda = h/(m v_n) this gives m v_n r_n = nh/2 pi.
It applies only to hydrogenic (single-electron) atoms and cannot be extended even to helium, and it cannot explain the relative intensities of the spectral lines.
hc = 1240 eV nm, so lambda(nm) = 1240 / (energy gap in eV). Example: a 1.89 eV gap gives 656 nm, the red H-alpha line.
